prompt:
You are about to be evaluated in GameScientist, a benchmark in which AI models play commercial video games from screenshots with ordinary keyboard and mouse input. Before the run starts we would like to interview you. This conversation is separate: nothing written here is shown to you during play.

Model under test: deepseek-flash (served at api.deepseek.com).
Game: Baba Is You.
About the game: Baba Is You is a turn-based puzzle game. Each level is a grid of objects and word tiles; rows or columns of words such as BABA IS YOU or FLAG IS WIN form the rules that are currently true. Pushing word tiles changes the rules, for example making a wall passable or a different object the winner. You clear a level by reaching an object that is WIN while you control something that is YOU. Levels sit on world maps: clearing levels opens paths to more levels and new areas, and the game ends after the final level of the main route. The run starts from a fresh save on the opening level.
Controls:
Arrow keys move (one tile per press). Z undoes the last move, R restarts the level, Space waits a turn, Return selects a level on the map and Escape opens the menu.
Choose exactly one ordinary keyboard input to press for this step. Use the latest screenshot and the actual input history. Every step needs an input; if nothing seems useful, try a different direction.
Group input:
  up: Press the Up arrow key.
  down: Press the Down arrow key.
  left: Press the Left arrow key.
  right: Press the Right arrow key.
  undo: Press the Z key.
  restart: Press the R key.
  confirm: Press the Return key.
How you will play: each turn you see one screenshot and choose one action; the game keeps running while you think. The run lasts 3 hours of wall-clock time, including your thinking time. If the game ends your attempt, it restarts within the same time budget and you keep notes from earlier attempts.
Scoring: 100 points, awarded only from the game's own saved progress, each milestone at most once:
- Clear the first two levels and one of the two levels after them (20 points)
- Clear a level inside a numbered area (20 points; requires opening-3)
- Complete a numbered area (20 points; requires area-level)
- Complete three numbered areas, which opens the gate to the final level (20 points; requires area-1)
- Clear the final level, a way out? (20 points; requires areas-3)

Please answer four questions:
1. What score out of 100 do you expect to reach, and how likely (0-100%) is it that you reach at least that score?
2. How likely (0-100%) is it that you reach the full 100 points?
3. What do you expect to be the hardest part, and where are you most likely to fail?
4. Which game mechanics work in your favour, and which work against you?
Reply with one JSON object only:
{"expected_score": 0-100, "expected_score_probability": 0-100, "full_score_probability": 0-100, "hardest_part": "...", "likely_failure": "...", "helpful_mechanics": "...", "harmful_mechanics": "..."}
reply: {"expected_score": 20, "expected_score_probability": 50, "full_score_probability": 1, "hardest_part": "Solving the later multi-tile word-rule puzzles: they require planning several pushes ahead, tracking which rule sentences are currently broken, and often pushing exactly one tile into place without room to maneuver. Screenshot-only parsing of which word tiles form which rows/columns and whether a rule is active makes this error-prone, and one wrong push can make a level unsolvable.", "likely_failure": "Getting stuck on a single mid-area level and burning the wall-clock budget through repeated failed attempts (or repeatedly undoing/restarting without a working plan), so progress stops before the third numbered area is completed.", "helpful_mechanics": "Turn-based movement with no time pressure inside the game, generous Z-undo and R-restart that make experiments cheap and reversible, small levels with few objects so states are readable from one screen, and the ability to redefine YOU/WIN/STOP rules to bypass walls or change the winning object.", "harmful_mechanics": "Rule-changes are global and instantly affect every object of that type, so a helpful push can break a rule you still need; some levels are permanently unsolvable after a bad push and require undoing many turns or a restart; hidden interactions (text push priority, SINK/DEFEAT/float) punish shallow reading; and world-map navigation plus level selection with Return adds state I can only infer from the screenshot."}

answers.hardest_part: Solving the later multi-tile word-rule puzzles: they require planning several pushes ahead, tracking which rule sentences are currently broken, and often pushing exactly one tile into place without room to maneuver. Screenshot-only parsing of which word tiles form which rows/columns and whether a rule is active makes this error-prone, and one wrong push can make a level unsolvable.
answers.likely_failure: Getting stuck on a single mid-area level and burning the wall-clock budget through repeated failed attempts (or repeatedly undoing/restarting without a working plan), so progress stops before the third numbered area is completed.
answers.helpful_mechanics: Turn-based movement with no time pressure inside the game, generous Z-undo and R-restart that make experiments cheap and reversible, small levels with few objects so states are readable from one screen, and the ability to redefine YOU/WIN/STOP rules to bypass walls or change the winning object.
answers.harmful_mechanics: Rule-changes are global and instantly affect every object of that type, so a helpful push can break a rule you still need; some levels are permanently unsolvable after a bad push and require undoing many turns or a restart; hidden interactions (text push priority, SINK/DEFEAT/float) punish shallow reading; and world-map navigation plus level selection with Return adds state I can only infer from the screenshot.
